speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to one point raised by my hon. friend I want to make it clear that professional people who were seeking admission to Canada during this movement were fully and carefully advised of the situation in Canada. Applicants, especially those in the professions, were required to sign a statement recognizing that they might not be able to practise their normal trade or profession and that they were willing to accept alternative employment should this be necessary.
This statement was made to all the professionals, including the Czech dentists, and indicated they fully understood that the licensing requirements in Canada were such that their entry into the profession was solely at the discretion of the licensing authority. May 26, 1969

including the United States, did not meet the necessary requirements. In some cases it will be necessary for them to take additional training in Canada, but that is outside the purview of this department. We are continuing to give these persons adjustment assistance and language training where necessary. Mr. Speaker, may I direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. Mr. Speaker, we have continuing consultations with professional licensing bodies in the provinces with respect to the admission of professionals from other countries. But standards are set by the professional bodies. In this case examinations were held or made available as a special concession. I understand that sixteen Czech dentists failed; in addition there were four from the United Kingdom, two from the United States and others from such countries as Ireland, South Africa, Norway and so on. I understand these people can re-apply for another examination in the Fall.
It is unfortunate if any professional has come to Canada with the impression that the situation is different from the existing one. I wish to assure my hon. friend that we have taken pains to advise these people in time of the situation, and we are taking pains to ensure they are receiving the best possible treatment in Canada. Nevertheless, standards are still a matter to be determined by professional licensing bodies.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate on the official languages bill was adjourned last Friday, I was saying that we are facing a grave danger, namely that bilingual districts are to be set up where services will be provided to the public in both languages.
Mr. Speaker, we agree. The public will be served by mere clerks, good French Canadians who, to be hired, will have to take a bilingual test and attend language courses.
As for English Canadians, they will continue to control the management and the administration of the billions of dollars allotted to the various departments and Crown corporations.
In fact, the bill will only increase the number of bilingual employees but will change nothing in the high management.
Equal partners in a new Confederation, yes, but not one-way. The "After me, you come first" attitude must cease or we will have to bring it to an end one way or another. It is for us to choose.
The bilingualism which the government has undertaken to apply appears like a defence of Canadian individuality and unity, within, against separatism in Quebec, without, against a too strong Americanization. This concept of bilingualism results from the mere juxtaposition of the two linguistic groups, along with a certain tolerance in the great public instead of a true understanding.
It is important to go further, to show more fairness, to allow each and every one to participate at all levels.
Mr. Speaker, this is what I was driving at in concluding my remarks.
No doubt you know that I have asked nearly 80 questions-in three separate groups- since the beginning of September, in connection with bilingualism in the public service. I
Official Languages
wanted to know whether there was a place for French Canadians in the Canadian public service or whether they were nothing but water carriers.
It is clear from the government's replies that they are just good enough to carry water, close doors and bring coffee. They give information to the public, occupy lower positions and get starvation wages.
However, higher management in all departments and Crown corporations is controlled only, and I emphasize the word "controlled", by English-speaking people. Unfortunately, the official languages bill does nothing to correct that situation.
Government members may argue that we must wait, that we must be patient, that changes are in the offing, that language courses are being offered. Yet I must say that language courses are in full swing since 1966.
But let us consider what has happened in the federal public service since 1966. I shall give you figures pertaining to the Bank of Canada, the Industrial Development Bank, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, Eldorado Mining, the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
As far as those Crown corporations or government agencies are concerned, the following can be noted:
The number of French-Canadian officials with those agencies has gone, from 6.9 to 5.6 per cent.
According to the figures from 1966 to 1968 we are not progressing but going backwards as far as our representation within the public service is concerned.
On the other hand, during the same period, the percentage of Enlgish-speaking civil servants employed by the same corporations increased from 88.6 per cent to 91 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, may I point out that within those very crown corporations, people whose mother tongue is neither English nor French outnumber those whose mother tongue is French. And for the posts concerned, a salary of $17,000 or more is paid.
I would like to know how the government proceeds in that field. Does it intend to assign the lower posts to all French Canadians and to give English Canadians the administrative and managerial positions? Could the government tell us whether it acts fairly with regard to promotion, reclassification and appointment to positions in the civil service for which a salary of $17,000 or more is paid?

May 26, 1969
Official Languages
I can quote figures to support this and I can give those figures to any hon. member. The government itself supplied those figures and they have appeared in Hansard. Unfortunately, no mention is made of that in the newspapers. I ask the Canadian Press and the Press Gallery reporters, not to speak about me, but to read in Hansard the answers supplied by the government since September. If they are conscientious, they will have to tell the truth to the public, namely that all French Canadians are considered fit for is to carry water or to give information to the public.
As for management, in all crown corporations and in all government departments, it is under the control of English-speaking people only.
As far as Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd. for example, is concerned let me quote some figures.
The proportion of French-speaking directors receiving $17,000 or more annually has not varied from 1966 to 1968; it has remained nil. In the same period and in the same crown corporation, I repeat in the same crown corporation, from 1966 to 1968, the number of English-speaking employees receiving $17,000 or more per year increased from 36 to 117.
There is a limit to being deluded with promises by prime ministers who tell us: Long live confederation, long live bilingualism. Keep quiet, you French Canadians, Quebecers, you will eventually get your place.
If we have to wait another 100 years to enjoy the rights granted to us by confederation, in 1867, I for one would prefer to get out of it. I am not prepared to wait another 100 years to know if we can have our place within confederation and the public service. If Canadians really want a bilingual, bicultural country, if we are really honest with ourselves, the ratios of 0 to 0 and of 36 to 117 will have to disappear, and not in five years hence, but right now, for our French Canadians brains will come less and less to Ottawa, and will rather develop their own state, because they will have no other choice.
I am willing to live in Canada, because I am no separatist, and I do not believe in separatism, and I say so sincerely, honestly, until proof to the contrary. But I do not believe either in the present confederation, or in this government who deludes us with bilin-gualism-biculturalism trifles, the application of which will change absolutely nothing, will contribute to increase the control by higher English-speaking officials, and will continue

to restrict the role of French Canadians to lesser positions in the public service, answering the public.
I think the population is unaware of the true situation. The people believes that this official languages bill will change the situation. I for one, think that it is all eye-wash, and that nothing in this bill guarantees that French Canadians will have their share of higher positions in the federal public service.
I could give you more figures for the Department of Finance, the National Research Council, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of Fisheries and Forestry, the Treasury Board, the Canadian Transport Commission and the Comptroller of the Treasury.
Among the senior officials earning $17,000 or over in the above-mentioned departments, the mother tongue of 40 only is French. On the other hand, the number of senior officials whose mother tongue is English reaches 518; this is a percentage of 6.6 per cent for French Canadians against 85.4 per cent for Englishspeaking Canadians.
The truly interesting point is to note the number of senior officials earning $17,000 and over and whose mother tongue is neither English nor French. The proportion is 8 per cent and the number, 49. Therefore, more citizens whose mother tongue is neither English nor French than French-speaking citizens are hired.
In 1965, Crown agencies and departments were administering more than 10 billion dollars. Mr. Speaker, that is big management. That is where the money of Canadian taxpayers goes. In my opinion, French Canadians are truly part of confederation, they are considered as very good taxpayers, and, consequently, they should have their share in the administration of those billions of dollars.
Mr. Speaker, we are subjected to much discrimination. We are ready to live through the tremendous adventure of confederation. We are ready to continue, for better or for worse. We do not want to take anything away from others, but we want our share. We do not want to create injustice for others but we want to be put on the same footing.
We do not want to be deluded into the belief that we are being treated in the same manner as English-speaking Canadians, we want to be first class Canadians at all levels of the public service, or else that body will continue to be what it is now: An ivory tower accessible only to English-speaking Canadians.
May 26. 1969

Mr. Speaker, many highly competent French Canadians-and I could name dozens of them-have complained to me about the injustices, the discrimination they were submitted to.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
When these very competent graduates from French-Canadian universities apply for a position in any department, and are turned down because they do not speak English, I say that is pure and deliberate discrimination on the part of certain narrow-minded English-speaking people in the public service who want to have control over the positions, when unilingual English-speaking applicants with the same qualifications get the positions.
Mr. Speaker, if our rules concerning the recruiting of civil servants are to be based on the degree of competence, I agree. But the language spoken should not be ground for discrimination because it would be the glaring proof that Confederation is not possible for French Canadians since they would be excluded from all senior administrative positions.
We are French-Canadian members in the federal parliament. I have been here since June 25, and I have the honour of representing my fellow-citizens from Lotbiniere. I do all my work in French, everything is done in French. Mr. Speaker, your mother tongue is French. Many hon. members have French as their mother tongue. There are many French Canadians in the public service, and thanks to the work the Ralliement Creditiste has done since 1962, we are respected in the federal parliament. The French fact is also recognized within the government.
However, Mr. Speaker, having French-Canadian ministers is not everything. In addition, the administration of the government, the leadership of the government-because we know that parliament is one thing and that the government is another-must be open to French Canadians.
We read and hear speeches from some separatists in the province of Quebec. I do not share their opinions; however, basically, I admire those people who stand up and say that the French-Canadian people should enjoy equal status. However, I fail to agree when they say that nothing can be altered in Ottawa and that separation has to come.
Mr. Speaker, I would like this government to prove that Confederation is viable and that the French-Canadian people can really have the positions they deserve in the public ser-
Official Languages
vice. I wish this government would, without depriving others, make it possible for us French Canadians to be treated as equals. Let us recognize both official languages, but let us also recognize the individuals who speak those two official languages; otherwise, Confederation will be meaningless.
Not only must we recognize both official languages-something that should have been done over a hundred years ago-but also the human beings who speak those languages. If those who speak one of these two languages are thrown out of the public service, 1 say that this bill is a lot of nonsense as well as the public service and Confederation.
It is up to us to prove to the whole world and to the Canadian people that Confederation is worthwhile, that it is possible within it to be respected and to respect others as well, to be considered on an equal footing without depriving one another, by recognizing, not only the official languages, but also-and that is even more important-those who speak them.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in the debate because regardless of the effect this bill will have on the nation as a whole it will place a burden on western Canada in addition to those already affecting the economic and social life of that part of the country. The bill represents an intrusion by this government into an area specifically reserved under the constitution, that is, the usage of the English and French languages.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) in his opening statement the other day said:
It is true that our constitution already provides for the use of both languages. At present, however, section 133 of the British North America Act applies only to the legislative assembly and courts of Quebec and to the federal parliament and courts. Though in no way amending the constitution, the bill which is being submitted to you does concern language usage in connection with the federal government and parliament and the institutions thereof. Seen in this light, the present bill represents the culmination of an extensive evolution.
The only way one can bring about an evolution of the constitution is by properly amending it; otherwise a written constitution is meaningless. Section 91 (1), an amendment to the constitution brought in under the St. Laurent government, restricts the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada as regards the use of English or French. It is obvious that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is trying to amend the constitution without the necessary consultation with the

a manner that will not impose a burden on our other groups. Throughout the years a tremendous fund of good will has been built up that is allowing this to happen. To impose at this time a bill of such a divisive nature into this climate of good will could very well destroy the purpose for which this bill is intended.
For that reason I oppose this bill unless it is first referred to the Supreme Court or is brought in as a proper amendment to our constitution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in the debate on second reading of Bill C-120 I want first to protest against the false and misleading reporting of this stage of the legislative process by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It was stated on the C.B.C. news program, "The World At Eight", on Friday morning that this measure could perhaps receive approval in principle by second reading later that day, and I understand that this statement was repeated again this morning. I also noticed that this morning's issue of the Globe and Mail, I believe under Mr. Seale's by-line, also repeated this misinformation. After almost five months of operation under the new rules, surely the persons reporting the proceedings of this house should know that second reading merely allows the referral of legislation to a committee and nothing else. However, in view of the fact that most members of the newspaper editors' fraternity in Canada appear to consider this debate to be almost totally unnewsworthy, perhaps one should be thankful that at least the people's broadcasting system deigns to mention it more or less in passing if only in an inaccurate way.
I should first like to deal with some of the most glaring trouble spots in the bill. The first of these is clause 13 (1) which says that a bilingual district may vary in size between a census district and a school district. The important thing to note here is that census districts are established by the Governor in Council and therefore can be quite variable in themselves. It seems to me that this bill has been presented to the public on the basis that bilingual districts will roughly correspond to the boundaries of federal electoral divisions even though it has been represented that British Columbia will have no bilingual districts and there would only be a few in the prairie provinces and Atlantic Canada excluding, of course, New Brunswick.
Official Languages
One could also ask what is the necessity of the establishment of bilingual districts at all in view of the proposed amendments to clause 9. The difficulty here, of course, is in the words "significant demand" because this is another area that is totally subjective so far as the administration of this bill is concerned. It is in the area of administration that the real troubles will arise because, as has already been pointed out by the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. McQuaid), the bill is in large part a purely administrative one and, apart from the clauses dealing with the administration of justice, does not give the federal government any new powers.
Many Canadians are already objecting to and are fearful of the emphasis being placed on bilingualism in the public service. One has only to refer to the comments of the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) for confirmation of this. It is my feeling that this bill will merely increase the emphasis rather than modify it or put it on a more rational and functional basis. I say this because I believe in bilingualism in the public service of Canada on a functional basis, but not in a totally bilingualized civil service. After all, what is the aim? I have always thought the aim to be that service should be provided in both languages. This does not mean that everyone must know both languages. It means that in any particular office or facility there should be one or more persons to serve the minority public in that area. However, everything about this bill seems to deny this reasonable policy, and on the contrary, implies an open-endedness that will force the provision of a bilingual service where it may not be desired or required. In this connection may I point to the fact that once established there is plenty of room for the expansion of bilingual districts but no provision for their abolition if, through the mobility of population, these same districts should no longer qualify for establishment as districts.
There is no provision for the desires of the residents to be heard. An advisory board is contemplated, but of what possible good is such a body if its members do not go out amongst the people actually affected by the board's opinion? Surely the board should reflect the opinions of the citizens concerned, or is this board to be just another haven for tired, worn-out Grits, another last chance for participatory democracy?
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The opinion of the editor of the Ottawa Citizen notwithstanding-and here I refer to

May 26, 1969
Official Languages
his editorial of May 22-the provisions of the bill concerning the administration of justice are particularly offensive to any understanding of our constitution, which of course places the responsibility for the administration of justice on the provinces. In its original draft, which is all we have before us officially, the provisions contained in clause 11 are flagrantly unconstitutional. How can this parliament impose a duty on any provincial court? To attempt to do so is to fly directly in the face of the doctrine of the division of powers and the supremacy of	parliament-doctrines
which are basic to our constitution. I suggest that the proposed amendment to 11(4) does not in any way get around this objection because it does not remove the duty mentioned in subclause 1 from any of the criminal courts of the common law provinces-that duty being to receive or take evidence in either of the official languages, depending upon the request of the accused. Surely the only effective way of curing this fault would be to make subclause 4 apply to subclause 1 in full.
No matter what the government says about clause 11, Mr. Speaker, and in particular about the way in which the subclauses are interrelated, there is no doubt in my mind that subclause 4 does not have any effect on subclause 1 by the interposition of subclause 3, because it is merely permissive in nature. In my opinion this is of particular importance in view of the coyness of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) in suggesting that it would place him at a disadvantage if he were called upon to defend this bill before the Supreme Court of Canada if he were to reveal his constitutional authority now.
The House of Commons is the highest court in the land, whether the Minister of Justice knows it or not, and I believe the minister is in contempt of this court by refusing to behave in an adult and mature manner in this regard. One would almost think he fancies himself as a Perry Mason type of person, saving all his legal expertise to the last possible moment. Speaking of expertise, one thing which is evident about this bill is that no drafting expertise went into it at all.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would now like to turn to the social implications of the bill. We have heard references made to melting pots and mosaics. Personally, I do not accept the melting pot theory as exemplified by the United States experience, as I believe the great significance of Canada is the tolerance displayed by the whole for its many parts. Of course, I speak as a member of that group of

Canadians whose background is neither British nor French. It may be, therefore, that I do not feel any guilt for any of the alleged sins of my forebears because, quite frankly, I do not feel guilty about any injustices which either the French or British allege may have been perpetrated on them by the other group in the past. Perhaps it is because they lack this guilt feeling that the people of western and most of Atlantic Canada cannot be said to be exactly in love with this bill. In these parts of the country it is looked upon as a central Canadian solution to a central Canadian problem. The only objection is that it has national implications and national repercussions totally outside the ambit of the Dominion civil service.
If one wants to look, plenty of evidence can be found that the Dominion government continues to believe it has the constitutional right to abuse its spending power, as it did with medicare, to impose its ideas on language and culture on the individual provinces. It would be interesting to know what economic or money lever was applied to the new premier of Alberta, Mr. Harry Strom, popularly referred to as a nice guy, to quieten that province's official if not actual doubts about this measure-doubts which were so ably set out by the hon. E. C. Manning in his letter to the Prime Minister of October 29, 1968.
Apart from constitutional or social questions I believe this bill raises questions important to Canada's economic future. While it is glib to say one cannot put a price tag on bilingualism because, according to its proponents, they have a monopoly on ideas for nation saving, I submit that there certainly is a price tag involved.
I referred earlier to the melting pot theory. In my view this bill will go a long way toward the imposition of the melting pot theory in this nation but with two pots instead of just one. This is twice as bad as having one. The bill before us will merely serve to weaken both the French and English languages in this country. I have had English speaking proponents of the bill tell me that it is a good bill because it will help to break down the relative immobility of the French speaking population of Quebec and get them out into the English speaking ocean of 220 million North Americans where they will be swallowed up and assimilated.
A further aspect of this bill which has not been considered, apart from the tremendous cost, is the inefficiency which it will cause.
May 26, 1969

This will make Canada, as a nation, less competitive in the world marketplace. I would like to refer here to what G. A. Blackburn, the man responsible for the federal service language training program, had to say as reported in the Montreal Star for April 16, 1969. I am reading from the report.
Becoming bilingual through classroom teaching is impossible, says the man responsible for the language training program in the federal civil service.
A second language, G. A. Blackburn said here yesterday, can only be attained by one who is prepared to work on a full-time basis in a second linguistic and cultural milieu for a long period- a year or more.
The need for the second language is particularly doubtful in the technological and scientific fields. I would seriously ask why these areas of the public service are not specifically exempt from the operation of this bill because surely it must be apparent to everyone that the average Canadian has absolutely no contact with these areas of the government. I believe it is also true that the French language has now become quite inadequate in these areas. It certainly cannot be argued that it is necessary to impose compulsory bilingualism on scientific and technological personnel in order to carry out the stated aims of this bill or to preserve and strengthen the cultural fact of the French language in this country.
I would like to make reference to the question of representation abroad. It should be apparent to everyone that for the next decade at least, if present policies are continued, more and more of the public service will be made up of persons whose first language is French. This will be one of the facts of life, because it is impossible for the rest of Canada, bearing in mind the facilities we have and the fiscal resources available to us, to produce anywhere near enough bilingual persons whose first language is English. I would again like to refer here to the comments of Mr. Blackburn as reported in the Montreal Star:
He admitted, however, that in his opinion the truly bicultural person is virtually non-existent. Even the bilingual person was "at an enormous disadvantage if he has to do intellectual creative work in a second language."
Stressing the differences between bilingualism and biculturalism Mr. Blackburn pointed out that England and the United States may speak the same language but they form two distinct cultural groups.
"They have most words in common, but the words do not necessarily mean the same thing."
Since language reflected the background and the experience of the people, communication between two individuals was effective only when they were of the same culture or when each of them had a
Official Languages
thorough understanding of the cultural background and experience of the other. "Failure to take this concept into consideration produces many translations which do not convey the intended message," Mr. Blackburn said.
He suggested that Canadian companies serving a clientele made up of both French and English "need a team representative of both cultures" with each member of the team "free to do his creative work in his own first working language."
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the question has to be asked: should not some attempt be made to define "bilingual" in order to relieve against this problem, because most of our representation abroad is of necessity conducted in the English language? Is it not poor practice to have policies at home which require our representatives abroad to work primarily in their second language? Will this policy give us our most effective representation where, as a nation which must trade to live, our interest is so vital? In other words, Mr. Speaker, will this policy help sell our timber, pulp and paper, fish, wheat and oil, or will it be a hindrance?

I believe the thoughts of one J. W. Kitchie of Victoria, British Columbia, are appropriate here, as he expressed them in a letter to the editor published in the Albertan of May 20, 1969. He says:
As the government has brought the new official languages bill before the House of Commons, and as there seems to be every indication that some appointments in the civil service, the armed forces and other federal agencies, will depend on a bilingual qualification it is essential that the term "bilingual" is clearly defined. The above definitions-
These are some definitions of bilingualism set out at the beginning of the letter to which I did not refer.
-are from two recent editions of French dictionaries, published in Quebec and in Paris. Three contemporary English dictionaries mention or infer equal facility, or fluency in both languages.
Complete fluency in both official languages will not be easy to find in this country; we must accept a degree of difficulty with idioms, the construction of sentences and some grammatical errors in that language which is not our native tongue. The Canadian of French parents often retains an accent to a greater or lesser degree which indicates his upbringing and background. Similarly, most English Canadians who have been taught French do not develop a true accent. Limited vocabularies and different grammatical constructions compound the problems. If one uses French with an English accent, some grammatical errors, a limited vocabulary and a lack of familiarity with French idioms, speaking only as well as some of the French federal cabinet ministers stumble through their television interviews in English, is one bilingual?

May 26, 1969
Official Languages
True bilingualism would be most difficult to achieve in this country, but practical bilingualism must be defined in the official languages bill to be equally fair to those seeking appointments where bilingualism is considered essential, whether their native language is French or English. Proficiency must be based on a standard, clearly defined ability to communicate regardless of the mother tongue of the individual.
Perhaps the most important aspect of the problem is forbearance and sympathy to someone who is seeking assistance, advice or direction in that official language which is not his mother tongue.
The Minister of Justice has stated that it would be tragic for Canada if this bill were referred to the Supreme Court for a test of its constitutionality. All I can say is that it is almost criminal for the minister to be promoting this bill and legislation such as the omnibus Criminal Code bill at a time when large areas of this country are suffering from what is in fact an economic depression due to the non-existence of an effective or aggressive grain marketing policy and abysmally poor administration of the grain movement machinery, while other areas are suffering from abnormally high unemployment compounded by the problems of runaway inflation and an inadequate housing program. I say it is almost criminal for him to be diverting our attention from these problems when he has so little faith in the legality of what he is promoting. After all, what would be so tragic about the Supreme Court of Canada declaring that this bill is perfectly within the powers of the government of Canada? I am sure we would all feel a lot more comfortable if that statement were made.
Even if the bill were clearly constitutional, since it deals with language it should be in our constitution, in the same way as religion. If there is the support for this policy in the country that the Prime Minister believes there is, and if he has the mandate he alleges, why is he avoiding its implementation through entrenchment in the constitution? He has already passed up the February, 1969, constitutional conference, and he could have used the one that is going to be held within the month for this purpose. Why is he ignoring that method in favour of using his parliamentary majority to force his ideas on the country?
In my view the people of Canada did not give the Prime Minister a mandate for this legislation at all. This legislation is really based on the two-nations concept which the Prime Minister never tires of saying was rejected by the people of this country last June.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not usually hesitant about entering a debate in the House of Commons, particularly on a controversial matter, but in this case I am. My reason is a fairly simple political one, namely, that I probably represent more French Canadians outside of the province of Quebec than anywhere else outside that province. The other day the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy) spoke on this measure, and I have been prompted to rise today because my interpretation of what has happened in that area over the years is considerably different from his. I had the opportunity of living in Timmins for many years. There are many people living in Timmins today who worked with me in the mines, having arrived in Canada from countries whose tongues were strange to that area. Many of these people now speak English with a broken accent. Many new Canadians came to the area from Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, the Ukraine, Hungary and many other countries, and they learned to speak our language very quickly because they had the obligation and the opportunity to do so.
The population of Timmins was a very heterogeneous one. People spoke their native tongue when they assembled, and I found Timmins a pretty good place to live because there was absolutely no discrimination on the part of anybody. It is interesting to note that the left wing and the right wing of each organization had its own hall and newspaper, but in the main the population of Timmins was fairly heterogeneous. Very little was said about language or religion, and very few were ever asked what was their ethnic origin.
I remember a survey carried out in a class that one of my children attended. According to that survey the largest ethnic group in the school, which I might point out was in the Italian section of the town, was Ukrainian, followed by English, Italian and French. Each of the following groups consisted of less than three pupils because there were only three Ukrainian children in the class. The teacher came from Africa and there were students from China, Japan and many European countries. I do not think the children found much of a problem in that area.
I worked for many years with these ethnic groups in Timmins and I found that their problems were identical with mine. They wanted more money. They wanted the boss to treat them better. They wanted a pension plan. These were the same things I and everybody else wanted. So in fact language
May 26, 1969

was not really the problem. If the hon. member for Timmins found things to be different, then I suggest that he made them different; it was not that they were different. I suggest that if you really want to find a problem you can always find one; otherwise there is no problem.
* (3:40 p.m.)
I am opposed to the attitude taken by a number of people in the province of Quebec, an attitude that is now spreading to Ontario and which I think will cause a great deal of grief to those sponsoring it. I refer to the establishment of unilingual French institutions in both Quebec and Ontario. If you go to a school in my area where French only is spoken, you have great difficulty in furthering your education. There are three institutions only to which you can go if you wish to take academic courses. But they are growing very rapidly and have too many students. Problems are developing in northern Ontario particularly because Laurentian University will not be enlarged quickly enough to admit all students seeking entry. I notice that the University of Ottawa has discussed this matter also. I read an article in the Globe and Mail saying that the university is not interested in becoming a unilingual institution but is happy to remain bilingual.
It is said that French speaking Canadians wish to remain unilingual in order to preserve their language and culture. Maybe that is correct; maybe it is not. English speaking people certainly do not have this attitude. I could, if I so wanted, include the letters U.E.L.-United Empire Loyalist-after my name. Seven or eight members here are United Empire Loyalists. It is therefore safe to say that English speaking Canadians are not of purely English descent in the sense in which our French speaking Canadians can trace an almost purely French descent. Our French speaking Canadians do not wish to belong to France but are conscious of their French heritage.
I was particularly impressed by the speeches of two hon. members, one of them being the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette). Over the years I have disagreed with his political views but I have always given him credit for representing the people of Quebec as I know them. He speaks for them, represents their aspirations, and when he says his constituents want to remain within the Canadian nation we should listen to him. If they are to be Canadians they cannot belong to another nation. That is the sense of 29180-573*
Official Languages
his remarks, although the translation I heard may have been of doubtful quality. He has said in English that the people of his area are interested in the development of Canada as a nation. That means that there is not much separatism in his constituency.
When the Minister of Justice was presenting a number of amendments to this bill the other day the hon. member asked him if he was as well informed about the attitude of English speaking Canadians as he was about the attitude of French speaking Canadians, and the minister said he was not. At least, that is how I understood his answer. It is difficult for us to know really what French speaking Canadians are saying, and an election in Quebec will not make us wiser. Although two or three new parties will contest future elections in that province, we will not know how the people really think on this issue because each party represents a different point of view. The people there Eire divided on some issues, and this is part of the problem.
In some ways the present government is dangerous. The Prime Minister, who is an academic, puts Quebec first. That has been his attitude for many years, I believe, and that has been the attitude of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) and, no doubt, of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand). Everyone is entitled to his position and I am condemning no one for taking sides on this very emotional and contentious question. But it is dangerous for these persons to take such a stand because no one is really clear about some of the things Quebec desires.
In my constituency there are some French speaking communities whose members are interested in exactly those things that interest all English speaking Canadians. French speaking farmers want exactly what English speaking farmers want. Last night I attended a meeting with French speaking and English speaking farmers. Both linguistic groups were concerned about a provincial Department of Highways program which was taking land from their farms. They all had exactly the same problems and faced them in exactly the same way.
I am afraid of the discrimination this legislation may promote in this country. The Prime Minister said that even elevator operators would need to be bilingual. Perhaps elevator operators need to know how to say "good morning" or "good afternoon" in both languages, but that is about as far as it goes.

May 26, 1969
Official Languages
If an operator is surly he need say nothing. Printed instructions and directions could be nailed to the sides of elevators, and no one would have to ask the operator for directions. In any event, it may not be a good idea to talk too much in elevators. People talking in the elevators may be slowing the service in the parliament buildings. I make these comments because some employees in Ottawa are worried about recent government actions.
In my constituency there are several communities in which French is spoken predominantly, although most of the people can speak and understand English. These people do not live in a ghetto. I mention these communities because I am pleased to see that the minister has recognized in the amendments he introduced how necessary it is to prevent the establishment of French speaking ghettos. In any event, establishing linguistic ghettos in this country would run counter to the spirit of the recommendations of the B and B report. When I visited Lac St. Jean recently and had a chance to refresh and enjoy myself I found no difficulty in communicating with the inhabitants. Therefore, why should ghettos be set up? It is unreasonable to expect older people to learn a second language. I have a neighbour who is French speaking and is proud to be French. She said to me at once, "You know, I was lucky to be born French." When I asked her why, she said, "Because I was forced to learn French. If I had not been forced I never would have learned it." Strange to say, her little son is doing poorly at school in French, finding it difficult to master.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
The Minister of Justice mentioned another criterion which struck me as being very odd. I would like to see it pursued when the bill reaches the committee stage. The minister named a number of Canadian universities and gave the number of graduates who had made applications for employment by the Civil service. The figures indicate there is employment in the civil service for university graduates. The minister should have mentioned how many of these positions carried a restriction of bilingualism. I would like Canada to be a bilingual nation but it is stupid to suggest that by tomorrow this country will be bilingual.
The government should change its attitude toward the constitution. The manpower service got more deeply involved in federal aid to education under program 5. When the present Minister of Regional Economic

Expansion joined the cabinet the program was scrapped. The education now provided by the provinces in this field is not nearly as satisfactory. The federal government should decide what education is required for the jobs available.
If the provinces are interested in establishing bilingual education, the federal government should make money available for this project. The government could start realistically providing opportunities for bilingual jobs in the civil service in 15 years' time when these students are qualified to do these jobs, but most persons trained in Ontario in the last 15 years are not capable of being bilingual. They may do as well as some of our deputy ministers who were trained at a cost of $45,000 but they will still follow the normal procedure of translating from one language to the other.
The Secretary of State says that federal education is unconstitutional and cannot be done. If the provinces were approached by the federal government with an offer to pay for bilingual education, I believe it would be accepted. When it is economically feasible, children of ethnic backgrounds should have an opportunity of learning more than two languages. When the government makes certain jobs available to bilingual people only, this is discrimination. If the federal government does not enter into some arrangement with the provinces to provide bilingual education, it will be discriminating against 85 to 90 per cent of our population.
The Minister of Justice stated he was in favour of the federal government providing financial assistance for bilingual education, but more than that is required. There must be an interest on the part of the Canadian people. Not all Canadians will be able to learn a second language. Some may even object to it. Most of us have prejudices of one kind or another. A child six years of age will have less prejudice than at 25 years of age. This is why it is important that bilingual education must begin in kindergarten. I suggest that four classes a day could be taught in one language and four in the other.
I strongly oppose the idea of hanging on to the province of Quebec as just a sop. When I say this I am speaking of the province and not of the people of that province. I am not in favour of the government making concessions merely to save its own skin. I have enough faith in the people of Quebec to know they will make up their own minds when the time comes. I suggest their decision will be based
May 26, 1969

on economic reasons. Those who want to separate Quebec from Canada suggest taking away the family allowance and other advantages. It is not necessary to discriminate against the rest of the country because of the province of Quebec. I do not know their attitude toward bilingualism, but I imagine they think the matter is being handled in a ridiculous manner. French speaking Canadians do not believe that bilingualism will really be put in effect. They feel it is not true bilingualism and are therefore not interested. English speaking Canadians will not be interested if their jobs are going to be in jeopardy.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) made some very good pronouncements respecting labour in the last few months. I am sure the minister agrees that a man is being violently discriminated against if jobs that might be available to him are not red-circled. His ability to develop six hands or four legs will be curtailed. Until a creature with four legs is available that job should be red-circled or everyone who does not have four legs will be discriminated against. This also applies to linguistic ability which cannot be developed overnight. If this legislation does not provide red-circle protection for jobs that require particular training, there will be discrimination that will apply to 75 per cent of the civil servants.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I believe that the federal government can make Canada a bilingual country. The only difference between us and the Americans is the Johnny Canuck atmosphere that we have maintained through the Don Messer show, the maple syrup jamborees, the Quebec Carnival. These are the kind of things that make us different from the Americans. Most of us feel proud of the image presented by the plaid shirts and the steel-capped boots of the lumberjacks. We have gained considerably from it.
I would be very surprised if any member of parliament disagreed with the theory that we should start bilingual education in kindergarten for future generations. I am sure that many members of parliament, and there are many who share some of my prejudices and have others of their own, would support this legislation if they were not certain it was going to move Hull into Ottawa and displace many of the English speaking people now working in Ottawa. This is the fear of many people. For some reason not many of my English speaking friends are bilingual. The only people who are truly bilingual are the
Official Languages
French speaking who have learned English. Thus we are faced with a major problem regarding employment in the federal civil service. I do not know that any of the senior English speaking officials are bilingual.
I am surprised at the attitude of some Liberal members with regard to some of the things that were accomplished in the past. It was not much to put bilingualism on cheques, but some laughed at the former prime minister because his regime accomplished that. I only wish they would stop to think of how things were when I first came to parliament. That is not long ago but even then, when a French Canadian stood up and spoke French in the house nobody listened, and it was four or five days later before his speech in French was printed in Hansard. Until the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) introduced the simultaneous translation system a French person did not speak in this house in French because by the time his speech was translated the debate was over.
Credit should be given for that action. It was an advance in communication. The reason I pay attention to my Social Credit friends who do not speak English is that now I can understand what they are saying. These have been worth-while steps. But no one should be of the opinion that we have to take all the steps at one time or we are not doing anything. Credit should be given where credit is due, and I am pleased to say that my experience shows there has been great tolerance shown in Canada to people of various ethnic backgrounds who came to this country. The only part of my ancestry that did not have any problem in coming to Canada contributed the small percentage of Indian blood that I have in me, but even those Indians of an earlier era would have felt out of place anywhere else except in the small territory they knew.
There are emotional reasons why some people can support this bin wholeheartedly and others cannot. If its only purpose is to create division, to give advantage to a particular group, we should not support that position. I also suggest that any government that hides behind the constitution and does not have the guts to stimulate bilingual education with federal support, direction and encouragement is being dishonest in sponsoring and passing this limited type of legislation. This legislation will make it very difficult for all adults today who speak only one language, and for all children going to school today in areas where bilingual educational facilities are not

May 28, 1969
Official Languages
available. Many of the people who have not supported this bill wholeheartedly have taken that stand because of their prejudice, but many of them have indicated that their children are going to schools where they will gain the advantage of becoming bilingual.
When my children were available for summer work they did not work in Ontario. They worked in Quebec. I have one son who worked in Quebec for four summers. When he went there to work on a job with 40 or 50 men, only the cook and the foreman could understand him in English. Surprisingly, after he worked there four summers everybody could understand him in English but he could not understand them very well in French. They had all learned English but he had not been able to learn French. So I sent another son to work in Quebec, and as he had learned his French in school he spent most of his time correcting their grammar. But at least we have made the effort. I am sure many people are willing to make the effort on behalf of their children and grandchildren.
However, these same people are disillusioned by a government that introduced this type of legislation out of bias and prejudice without simultaneously introducing legislation giving bilingual opportunities to all Canadians. I hope that before long the Minister of Justice will have his way in cabinet. I am sure the Minister of Labour and a number of his other English speaking colleagues will support that position and provide an opportunity whereby the provinces can take advantage of federal assistance to establish a bilingual educational system for all their people. I strongly urge the government to explore the possibilities of supplying the kind of financial assistance that will allow the provinces to make bilingual education an accomplished fact in all of Canada.

speechtext:
approach based, I am sure, on honest instincts. As I said, there is a high degree of emotionalism, some of which is healthy, much of which is based on friendship-friendship with individuals-and some based on a love of this country as it is, as it has been, and what we hope it to be.
I have lived in Quebec, where I brought my bride from England. I have fought side by side with French speaking citizens of this country during the war. My brigade was a half French speaking union of Le Regiment de la Chaudiere and the North Shore New Brunswick Regiment. I have joined in the political activity of this country, as well as in business and private life, with our French speaking compatriots. I have done these things with men with names such as Metivier of St. Damien de Bellechasse, Lainesse of St. Hyacinthe, Tessier of Toronto, Letoumeau of Montreal, Beaudoin of Valcourt, Leclaire of Granby, and Huel of Gravelbourg, Saskatchewan. Like the hon. member for Timiskaming, my children have worked on the roads and in the factories of Quebec. They too have very close friendships and certainly we are all proud of these friendships.
Today I serve with men like Pilon, Laniel, Clermont and Dr. Isabelle, and under men like Pepin, Marchand, Pelletier and Trudeau. I serve also with men across the chamber such as Caouette and Latulippe. Perhaps I do not agree with them all the time. But I respect them and the quiet dedication of the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin), with whom we all mourned in his recent tragic loss. To be unemotional in such circumstances would be less than human, but anything that lessens such associations I oppose with all my vigour and anything that brings us closer together I cherish and revere, and I will fight continuously for these things in this house.
While this bill represents a milestone it also represents opportunities not suggested in the bill itself. It represents an opportunity for mutual enrichment, for dignity and for a distinctive Canadianism. I was rather interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Temiscamingue. We think of ourselves as a nation and are respected as a people throughout the world. We have this great magnetic force in that great nation to the South whose people are our great friends, allies and business partners. Yet there is something special about being a Canadian. We have rejected the melting pot tradition they have adopted, and maybe this is a natural evolution in view of
Official Languages
the fact that our great immigration took place after theirs.
In my own area of Toronto, which is a great centre of massive immigration to this country, there is no thought of calling people names based on their origin, as happened in pre-war times. We used to comment on their accents, but today we take pride in their existence here. We enjoy the opportunities which exist for mutual enrichment and we enjoy their traditions, their restaurants, their churches and their parties. This is a shrinking world because of modem transportation where by people of this country can be in another country or another continent or environment in a matter of hours.
We must always remember the advantages that may accrue to us as a result of bilingualism. This may not be true of many of us, but many of our children will become bilingual and many will become trilingual as a result of the language of their parents. This will not only make us a favored people as world citizens but more favoured in this country. It will be of assistance to our economy in the world, and our children welcome this bill.
The people I have spoken to across this country from east to west have certain reservations for themselves in this regard but no reservations for their children. I have yet to meet a teenager-a schoolboy or schoolgirl- who does not welcome this as an opportunity. These are the ones we are really working and talking for today.
In the short time I have been here I have found that progress comes slowly. It is important, however, that we continue to make progress in view of the opportunities that we have. We think of the opportunities for travel our children have as a result of the supersonic and jumbo jets now coming. Our children will spend their weekends or vacations in various areas of the world. We must remember the advantages our children will have in speaking another language when visiting other parts of the world. This will be of tremendous advantage to them.
I must say in passing that if the future unity of this country was dependent on my ability to speak the French language we would be in deep trouble. I will be taking a total immersion course beginning next week and I fear I may drown, but I hope that following it I will be more conversant with this language. At least we are trying. Many members of this house are making an effort, and this is very important.

May 26, 1969
Official Languages
These great things will not happen as a result of the passing of this bill, but by surpassing this bill. The conscious decision that we should accept this as a fact of Canadian life and as one of the advantages and enrichments of life in this country sets the stage for future development. This is not going to happen immediately, as I said. It might not happen in our lifetime. We may not see bilingualism during our time, but hopefully we will see progress to the point that in another generation 20 per cent of the non-French speaking population will be bilingual. Perhaps in still another generation there will be a 50 per cent improvement over the situation as it is now. This conscientious decision we make now sets the stage for the future.
This decision will require patience and tolerance not only on the part of the English speaking but also on the part of the French speaking people. We often think we are the ones being asked to show tolerance, but I believe there is another side to that coin. If we show determination and sensitivity we will enjoy progress. There are those within the province of Quebec and outside that province who want to see change overnight. I do not think any reasonable person in any part of the country expects that to happen.
This whole change could be endangered by carelessness and intemperance within and outside the House of Commons, statements on this side of the house as well as on the other side, by backbenchers as well as frontbenchers. There is sometimes a brittleness involved in our approach to this matter which we should avoid at all costs.
We must make the right choice and adopt the right attitude not only for ourselves but primarily for the new generation. We must think in the future without reaching into the past. Talk of 100 years of oppression is no more constructive than talking of 100 years of introversion. It is mutual respect, mutual interest and mutual opportunity such as is being shown at this time which should motivate us. We are dealing now with the basic rules of the game. The rules of the game combined with wise government and the implementation of this type of thought can weld us into a vital and unique nation. We must develop a nation that utilizes the very best within us and utilizes all of us to the maximum of our potential. We must develop a nation where by mutual affection, respect and enrichment, with sensitivity and determination, we can set an example for our future generations and an example for other nations to emulate.

[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)

I suggest that with the staff he has at his command, and with his knowledge of English, the explanation he has just given will receive the attention it deserves. In the same speech he also said:
We intend to restore full citizenship rights to the two linguistic majorities.
What are the lost citizenship rights that are going to be restored? Restoration implies existence, usage and alteration. I would like to hear him clear that up when he speaks. He said again on another occasion, "We will restore full citizenship rights". He also produced that old chestnut that he used during the days of war-I will not quote him any more unless he wishes to challenge me-when he spoke about the siege mentality of French Canada as a result of the attitude of the rest of Canada. I never saw that siege mentality. French Canadians have served during both the first and second world war with distinction and greatness. What does siege mentality mean? Was that designed to be tolerant and objective?
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
He has been known to be the sworn enemy of anything in our country that is in the British tradition. That has been his attitude throughout. Do you know what he calls it? He has one of these intellectual words for it. He calls it "euthanasia". He says there are things

we should not have around that are like certain structures that have outlived their usefulness. So the best solution is euthanasia. That is the explanation for his attitude to our British traditions. That is the explanation of the attitude which he has toward those who believe in the monarchy which gave to French Canada under the British Crown, and before it was in any way the Crown of Canada, equality of religion. When it was denied in the United Kingdom it was given by the Crown in Canada in 1775, and those people who but 20 years before had found themselves under a different monarch saved Canada for the British Crown in 1776. We see all the time this whittling away and cutting away at British traditions while we hear such phrases as "let us be tolerant, let us be reasonable".
I have here another statement which he will say was translated incorrectly. This is really a phrase which caps them all from a department from which translations have become untranslatable. It is a Museums of Canada press release entitled "Aboriginal Art". It reads:
A magnificent exhibition of Canadian aboriginal art will go on display at the Mus6e de l'Homme in Paris on March 25-
Canada will be represented by an official party headed by Secretary of State Gerard Pelletier who will open the exhibition. The party will include both Canadian and French cabinet ministers.
Was that wrongly translated? The silence gives the answer.
I wish the presentation had been made by the Minister of Justice. As I said a moment ago, he knows parliament. He does not look down from the heights of ivory towers on ordinary human beings. He meets parliament as parliament should be met. The Minister of Justice presented his case and the house listened. I am not in agreement with several of the arguments he made, but he treated parliament as though it was parliament, not as though it was a place in which to be taught of the new Canada.
We are dealing with this matter at a time when there are economic problems facing Canada the like of which we have not faced. Yet our time is taken up by the government of Canada with homosexuality, abortions, and now with this bill, a large portion of which has already been carried into effect long before it was ever brought before the House of Commons.
The same thing is happening all over Canada. There is the most callous disregard of western Canada by this government. They

laughed at western Canada when the Prime Minister said: "What do you expect me to do, sell wheat?" The wheat piles up. The position of farmers today has never been worse since the darkest days of the drought and lowest world prices. The government tells us, "Just give us time. We are thinking about it. We are waiting for a report from someone." They do not know what the western farmer wants. This is how serious the situation is. This is what was written in the latest issue of the Western Producer:
We charge the Trudeau government with callous neglect of the problems of the farming industry, particularly in the prairie region. Action should have been taken weeks ago, at least on such policies as might have provided farmers with a few clues as to how to carry on and what to grow. There was enough evidence to justify such action, long before the agricultural committee toured the west, but the opportunity has been missed.
There are, of course, possible moves that will be of some help to some farmers. But unless something is done quickly the ruination of thousands of farmers is a certainty.
While the farmers are in this situation the government produces a bill that, so far as the bilingual portions of it are concerned, had been put into effect all along the line before it ever received consideration from parliament. Think of the old soldiers, commissionaires, who were thrown out. Think of those who, having served for years in the civil service, stand in deep fear.
A budget has been promised for the beginning of June. The resolutions based on the last budget have not been put before the house and the government has been unlawfully exacting taxation for all these months. What manner of people are they? Are these our masters? There are two or three of them who understand parliament, and two of them are in the front row now. Some of the others do not. I will not restrict it to those two, but they happen to be in the front seats, and there are only three others so it would not take very long to gather who they are by elimination.
Surely the government must bear the yoke of responsibility for its failure to act. It is taxing illegally month after month and now it is getting ready for another budget. We are getting them so often now it is difficult to say which is which, particularly when those which have been introduced have not yet been passed. My point is that this bill was not needed and that the government has played fast and loose with the introduction of measures that have not received any support from parliament.

I will not attempt to cover any of the ground that has been covered. One of the benefits of being in bed is that you have time to read everything and you know all the arguments that have been advanced. I do not intend to repeat them except for the apologia of the Minister of Justice on whether or not this bill as a whole is unconstitutional. He said: "It is constitutional, the Prime Minister says it is." On the other side there is that former Liberal minister, Mr. Thorson, an apostle of Liberalism through the years who occupied the second highest position in the judiciary of Canada and who says it is unconstitutional. What does the minister say to that? He says: "It is not. Pierre says it isn't. Why should we go to the courts? Why should the matter be submitted to the courts? Language is a matter of politics, not law." But the right to language is a matter of law under the constitution, and the reason they have gone about it in this way to bring in a bill which is not what the B and B Commission recommended-that institution has had $8 million worth of sittings and came out with the recommendation that there should be a constitutional amendment-is that they could not get such an amendment.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I do not know who the person was-and I would not think of looking around, even to one who does not pay attention to what is being said-but I have come to the conclusion that whoever produced certain portions of this bill must have had a wide knowledge of Machiavelli.
I intend to deal for a few moments with the major portion of this bill, the clauses dealing with the commissioner, that is to say, clauses 19 to 34. Somebody asked me: What is the principle of this bill? Mr. Speaker, the principle of this bill is the coercion and intimidation which can be practiced by this man who will occupy the position of commissioner-I was about to say commissar. But no commissar was ever given greater powers than this commissioner is to receive.
He is to be "the Commissioner of Official Languages for Canada, hereafter called 'the Commissioner'." That was the recommendation of the B and B Commission. He was to be an ombudsman with the conscience of Canada in his possession. Well, if they had appointed a man like that I could not have any objection. But let us see what his powers are to be. It will be interesting to see who will be recommended, because there has been a search on. It would not be hard to find a

person here who has a dictatorial bent, to assume the post provided the salary is as promised. Let us examine the way in which the appointment will be made and how it is to come about.
The bill says that the appointment shall be made by parliament. And that is the end of everything. When parliament appoints him, the belief will be held among the people that, after all, his position will be like that of the Auditor General who, incidentally, does not enjoy a very high reputation in Liberal circles as a result of some of the findings he has made. This man will have powers the like of which have never been given to anyone before. Parliament is to appoint him, provided he does the job the Secretary of State wants him to do. In the event of the death or resignation of the Commissioner while Parliament is not sitting or if he is unable or neglects to perform the duties of his office, the Governor in Council... may appoint a temporary commissioner-
Is this man going to enjoy independence, Mr. Speaker? Can you imagine the Secretary of State, with that beneficient attitude he has shown, saying to this man: "We do not agree with what you are doing but we are going to keep you on"? There is a right to replace him at any time between sessions.
What will his powers be? This is tremendously interesting, too. He may appoint such officers as he deems proper and fitting, provided he has the consent of the Treasury Board. or agency of the government, the R.C.M.P., the army-or the Canadian Armed Forces; I do not know whether it will be necessary to be completely bilingual in order to serve in the Canadian army once this bill has been accepted. He has sole discretion. How many of you appreciate that parliament itself can be investigated by him? At this sole discretion he may investigate the administration of parliament itself. What is the idea of this? What dictator could ask for more than these powers which are being sought from the parliament of the people? At his sole discretion the commissioner may regulate the procedure to be followed in carrying out investigations. He may disclose in his reports only such matters as he alone decides shall be disclosed. Sir, such powers have never at any time been asked for previously. Those opposite have not had the effrontery to do so. I can understand now why it was not the Minister of Justice who introduced this bill.
There are other clauses here to which I should like to refer. There is the clause which gives the power to investigate parliament. Let us get ready to make a salaam to this almighty voice we are setting up in this legislation. Remember, you are all asked to vote for this; you are all to get down and say yes to this legislation in the interest of Canadian unity. It does not matter what we give away; we must support this bill because if we do not the Secretary of State will say we are bigots.
Let me go on. It says this:
The Commissioner shall investigate any complaint made to him to the effect that in a particular instance or case the status of an official language was not or is not being recognized or the spirit and intent of this act was not or is not being complied with-
If, in the course of investigating any complaint it appears to the Commissioner that having regard to all the circumstances of the case any further investigation is unnecessary he may in his discretion refuse to investigate the matter further.

Here is one; when we read of Mr. Justice Stewart's judgment the day before yesterday, in which he dealt with the legislature of Ontario, we find it is child's play compared with this. The next provision is:

Where the Commissioner decides to refuse to investigate or cease to investigate any complaint, he shall inform the complainant of his decision and may, if he thinks fit, give his reasons therefor.
This man is being put upon a pedestal. He may be removed by joint resolution of parliament, yes; but which of the members supporting the government of Canada would ever vote for his removal, no matter what he did? He becomes the "Charlie McCarthy" for the minister, who will be the head of this particular phase of our development. We know that the minister is the Secretary of State because the government wants somebody who understands everything but parliament.
That provision includes the words "if he thinks fit". People used to complain about the Star Chamber, but we will have no cause to complain at all if we vote in favour of this legislation.
The next provision is:
Every investigation by the Commissioner undei this act shall be conducted in private.
How many members have read the powers that we will be handing away, however estimable the objective and generally acceptable? Then, clause 28 (2) provides:
It is not necessary for the Commissioner to hold any hearing and no person is entitled as of right to be heard by the Commissioner-[DOT]
And hon. members are going to vote for this! How many of them have read the major portion of this bill? The provisions to which I have just referred indicate that, however thick the gloss that has been put on the bill, its principle is that of coercion. Let me read on. After the Commissioner has made his mind up, it is provided:
-he shall, before completing the investigation, take every reasonable measure to give to that individual, department or institution a full and ample opportunity to answer any adverse allegation or criticism-
So first the Commissioner finds a person or a department guilty and then he says: "I want to be fair; I should like to hear your side of the story." I ask hon. members whether they are going to grant him such powers.
Then in order to make it possible for him to expand beyond all limits, though I cannot

think of any additional powers that he would ask for, it is provided:
Subject to this act, the Commissioner may regulate the procedure to be followed by him in carrying out any investigation under this act.
Clause 30 provides:
The Commissioner has ... power (a) to summon and enforce the attendance of witnesses and compel them to give oral or written evidence on oath-
The Commissioner is not satisfied with that because he is then given power-
-to receive and accept such evidence and other information whether by oath or by affidavit or otherwise as in his discretion he sees fit-
What manner of men are these who produced this document? The Commisioner may receive evidence under oath or not under oath. This section applies where, after carrying out any investigation under this act, the Commissioner is of the opinion that an act or omission that was the subject of the investigation is or was or appears to be or have been
(a)	contrary to the provisions of this act;-
That I can understand.
(b)	contrary to the spirit and intent of this act but in accordance with the provisions of any other act of the Parliament of Canada-
This would mean that even though a department of government were acting pursuant to an act passed by this parliament and in effect, the Commissioner could repudiate and condemn action taken. Hon. members are being asked to vote for this provision. This kind of thing cannot be justified. I do not care on which side of the house an hon. members sits: those regulations deny the fundamental rights of an individual and can only lead to witch-hunts across this country of such magnitude that McCarthy would appear almost a novice by comparison-and he certainly is an unlamented memory.
Clause 33 (2) provides:
The Commissioner may disclose in any report made by him under this section such matters as in his opinion ought to be disclosed in order to establish the grounds for his conclusions and recommendations-

The Minister of Justice had gone through western Canada and had spoken with the various Attorneys General. I do not know how they do it, but the press always seem to know what is going on, and they reported that there was an awful fight in cabinet. The Commissioner may, instead of making a separate report to Parliament. .. include such report in his annual statement to Parliament. .. unless, in his opinion, the nature of the reuort is such that it ought to be brought to the attention of Parlia-men without delay.

This bill places in the hands of a commissioner who will be the puppet of the government the power to do all these things. If the commissioner does not do these things to the satisfaction of the Secretary of State, then as long as parliament is not sitting somebody else may be substituted. Somebody might ask: Do you think they would really do that? Well,
I have just read what the Prime Minister said at his press conference, as reported in the Ottawa Journal of October 17. The Prime Minister was asked what would happen if an English speaking civil servant said he was unwilling to learn French. As reported in the press the Prime Minister said:

We d say fine .. . We'll keep you running elevators where there are no French Canadians.
It is said that the Prime Minister made this comment frivolously. Under the laws of evidence, and we follow the British common law, ejaculations are always taken as evidence, even when they are hearsay, as indicative of the thinking of the person making them.
Some one asked what would happen if the commissioner does not act properly. Well, the
