speechtext:
It is important to know the background of certain things because I think all hon. members on both sides of the house wish to see a greater degree of unity in this country. We all want our peoples to live together and work together as Canadian citizens. Certainly there is great need for us to communicate with each other in this country in order that we may better understand and appreciate each other's attitudes and feelings.
A little story may illustrate the point I am trying to make. A close friend of mine has a son going to university and during the summer months the young man worked with a construction crew, shoulder to shoulder with those who labour in trades so necessary for the construction industry of our country. He was under a foreman who did not speak English very well. The foreman said to the lad: "It really does not matter. In this job there is only one word that counts-shovel." According to the story the foreman said, "When you say 'shovel' I will give you the shovel, but when I say 'shovel', you use it". I think that story illustrates how our peoples must communicate with each other and understand one another. In my opinion all hon. members, regardless of where they sit, wish to see a greater degree of unity in this country and want our peoples to communicate better with each other.
May 26, 1969



I do not think that Bill C-120 will unite this country. I believe it will divide us further and therefore I find it very difficult to support. I have French speaking and English speaking friends as well as friends in most other ethnic groups across Canada. I have travelled the length and breadth of this country and consider myself a loyal Canadian. I wish to see the country united and strong, and I wish all Canadians to understand the necessity for our unity and strength.
I agree that the Prime Minister has some claim to a mandate in introducing this bill. He did not talk very much about general policy in the election campaign, but he did talk about language policy. He also tried to condemn the Conservative party for a two-nation theory, saying that theory would divide the country. Yet I do not believe he has a mandate to flout or override the law of this land as expressed in our constitution, the British North America Act. I am not a legal authority but I know that some of our best legal brains, as well as provincial premiers, have questioned the legality of this bill. It troubles me to see the Prime Minister adopt inflexible attitudes based on the constitution when it comes to questions of housing. He was willing to see the deputy Prime Minister resign from the cabinet as he invoked constitutional arguments on questions of housing. However, when he comes to this bill he ignores the constitution he has previously upheld so firmly and tries to convince us that it does not really matter, that we need not consider whether this bill is legal, and that we need only be concerned with making passage of this bill politically possible so that we can have two official languages in this country.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I do not understand this attitude. It troubles me. I believe there is a very special and unique place in Canada for the French and English languages in the historical sense, but to establish French and English as the two official languages must be done through constitutional reform. Having done that, if necessary certain legislation could be introduced to verify it so far as the laws of the country are concerned in interpreting the constitutional aspect. I believe that would be in the best interests of this country. I say, with respect, to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) that we are being forced at this time, for whatever reasons or motives the government may have,
Official Languages
to deal with a bill that raises serious questions so far as the constitutional legality is concerned.
I say again I am not against English and French being the official languages of this country. I wish it were possible for every Canadian citizen to speak both French and English. I do not happen to belong to either one of those two language groups, speaking the language of my father which I learned as a boy. In my foreign experience I have had the opportunity to learn and use several other languages to the extent that I am fluent in understanding and using them.
In some parts of the country there is no opportunity to receive an education in French and English at the time when it is most effective, in childhood. Some Canadians do not have the opportunity of becoming fluently bilingual. This is true for both French and English speaking Canadians. To enforce this legally through legislation will divide us, not just in western Canada but also in Quebec. Many of my colleagues in this house who are from Quebec speak in favour of this bill, but many of my friends and acquaintances in Quebec have no real enthusiasm. I have not seen nor heard anything to indicate that the present government of Quebec intends to force this bill with all its implications even though it specifically relates to the federal government.
There are reactions in other parts of Canada as well, not only from those who are English speaking but also from those who are French speaking. There is very little support for this bill in French speaking communities outside the province of Quebec. In fact the contrary is true. Many such people are fearful that the enforcement of this bill in a linguistic way will take away from them the opportunities they already have at the present time. People who live in strictly English speaking areas of the country as well as those who live in strictly French speaking parts of the country feel this bill is not desirable because it will give a basis for a legal interpretation where at the present time there is a great reservoir of voluntary good will.
The English and French languages should be taught in such a way that when students finish high school and go on to university they will be fluent in both languages. My own family live in this city. My children attend school in this part of the country in order to become fluent in both languages. In western Canada there is a great dearth of French speaking teachers. Some people say there is

May 26, 1969
Official Languages
more antagonism to the use of French in Alberta than in any other province. This is not the case at all. There was a French language teacher training college in Edmonton before there was a similar institution in any other part of Canada, with the exception of the province of Quebec. Because the province of Alberta could not recruit sufficient French teachers from Quebec or teachers fluent in the French language from other parts of Canada, they began to train their own teachers of French. Alberta has even sent recruiting teams to France in an effort to recruit French teachers who would adequately and properly teach the French language in the schools of Alberta.
Our beloved Governor General grew up in and is a native of my city of Red Deer. He has told me that when he went to high school there was no opportunity to learn the French language. A short generation later when I went to school, French was being taught beginning with grade nine. My own children went to the same school and started learning French in grades four and five. This is progress-willing and substantial progress!
We have come a long way. Instantaneous translation in this house was a tremendous step forward to the effective use of languages in parliament. This is a constitutional right because it is outlined in the British North America Act. This is the kind of progress we will continue to make as long as we retain and develop the growing good will in this country at the present time in understanding the language, cultural and other needs of individuals in their various situations and backgrounds.
I feel this bill will divide rather than unite us. While I may agree with the principle stated by the Prime Minister and others as being the objective of this bill, I do not think we will move toward that objective nearly as effectively as we are now proceeding. It would be more effective to establish a constitutional change in a proper context respecting the use of languages.
In Great Britain students with a secondary school and university education have learned a second language. In fact, most people in Great Britain speak two or three languages, French, German, Scandinavian or whatever their desire may be. This is also true in France where most young people learn to speak English, Spanish, Italian or German. It is certainly true in the Scandinavian countries and in Germany, Holland, Belgium and even Russia. These people are doing this willingly.

We in this country have been backward in our outlook toward a second language, and this must and will change.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The foremost second language in this country must be French. There must be encouragement, incentive and motivation so that we may continue to grow and develop until we reach a position of being truly a bilingual people. I know it is not possible for everybody to learn a second language. One cannot gain mastery of a second language without using it, and there are parts of Quebec, western Canada and other regions where there is no opportunity to use a second language. Thus not everybody can become fluently bilingual.
There are some who say that civil rights must be applied to this bill because the real intention is to apply civil rights as they pertain to language by having a law such as this. If this is so then civil rights must be extended also to other languages such as Ukrainian, Polish, German and Spanish. We must have the civil right to use the language of our choice, but I do not think we can enforce the kind of civil rights that might be interpreted as being contained in this bill.
I am concerned about the provisions in the bill with respect to the definition of language districts. There is some detail in it which says that these districts shall coincide with municipal, provincial, federal or electoral districts, but there is no specific statement on the limit of a language area, or as to the authority who would be ultimately responsible for defining it.
There is another aspect of the bill which concerns me, relating to the Armed Forces and the R.C.M.P., an aspect that is brought out very clearly in some of the proposed amendments. Defence forces and the national police come directly under the federal government. Does this bill mean that in the future I or my children must be bilingual before we have the right to fight for this country? Does it mean that only those who are bilingual can be members of the R.C.M.P.? I do not see that the bill states anything to the contrary, even in the proposed amendment that is supposed to clarify the situation.
Since this is the interpretation given to the bill in layman's language I can understand that there are genuine fears throughout the country. These fears exist in and toward the civil service as well. People in the provinces
May 26, 1969

of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Newfoundland and elsewhere just do not have opportunities to become fluently bilingual even though they take French for seven years in elementary and high school, simply because usage is so important to bilingual fluency. I have no doubt that a very serious impediment will be placed upon those people in the civil service who are unilingual, and upon people who do not have sufficient fluency in a second language to be eligible for posts in the Armed Forces and other federal civil service branches.
I wish the Prime Minister had shown the same concern in taking steps to establish a national capital area to include the immediate area around Hull and Ottawa, an area which could be clearly specified as bilingual so that English and French speaking people coming to it would feel equally at home. If this were done it would go a long way toward achieving the degree of desirable bilingualism that we want to see in Canada, without interfering with provincial authority or bringing undue pressure on unilingual parts of the country.
In such a case I do not think French or English unilinguists could have any objection. It would also be a real incentive for the civil service, the Armed Forces, the R.C.M.P., crown agencies and all other aspects of federal administration. There are other ways in which we could move to encourage greater use of a second official language and its establishment as something practical, ways of encouraging rather than forcing people into a certain position. That is why I am convinced that this bill, instead of being one, as has been said, intended to unify and establish civil rights, is one that will defeat those very things which we all mutually agree are desirable in Canada.
The Prime Minister has warned against racial distrust and has said it would split the nation forever. I do not think the vast majority of the Canadian people really believe that this bill will remove that distrust and strengthen the understanding and communication we need. Despite our differences of opinion I believe that behind the thinking, motivation and objectives of all of us there is a desire to see Canada grow in unity. From my own world experience I often say to myself, if we cannot find the key to unity in Canada what hope have we in the world of having peace and understanding?
I am afraid that what is happening is that we are dividing and balkanizing ourselves, and instead of being the hope and example to
Official Languages
the world we are falling far short of that objective. I appeal to all hon. members on both sides of the house to look at this bill objectively, to look at it from the standpoint of how it will affect unity in this country, and to understand that there are two sides to the question. If they can see the thing as I see it and as many others see it, some who have spoken and some who have not, then I believe there will be agreement that this is not the strengthening factor that others think it might be.
Confederation in Canada is a marriage. It is a marriage of peoples. The type of marriage that is based on legal interpretation of rights and duties will inevitably end in bickering and ultimately wind up in the divorce court. If we can persuade our fellow Canadians that for the sake of our homeland tolerance and good humour, forgiveness and understanding are the practical and essential needs of any longlasting association, then we will find an answer to the problems we face.
I think this is the answer to the question of language rights. It is only on this basis that we will reach that degree of unity which is necessary to make this country strong in the future, as she has been in the past, with a role to play that the world needs as an example. Again, Mr. Speaker, I regret very much that I cannot see this coming about so far as language is concerned through Bill C-120.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very interested in some of the comments that have been made respecting this bill this afternoon because it seems that every member who participates in the debates, whether he is for or against the provisions of the bill, prefaces his remarks by saying that we all have to do something to strengthen the unity of the nation. However, what follows seems to be somewhat contradictory with respect to what in fact are the positive actions that will lead to a greater degree of unity.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) again displayed his mastery of the role of opposition, and I respect him for that. I think we have to recognize that what he tried to do, very unsuccessfully in my opinion but there was some reaction and response to his argument, was state the extreme. He tried to put the most extreme interpretation on the powers granted the language commissioner. Of course, the right hon. gentleman knows very well that if

May 26. 1969
Official Languages
you were to give the most extreme interpretation to any of the powers granted to those people charged with the responsibility of administering the laws of this land you could arrive at some of the almost ridiculous conclusions which he tried to advance in this house. Of course, part of the job of the opposition is to point out that such powers can be abused if an extreme interpretation is placed on these words.
I hope this bill will be sent to the committee soon so that the committee will be able to examine in greater detail, with the ministers who are piloting this legislation through the House of Commons, some of those things that will be needed to give effect to the principle that is involved.
I may say I accept the broad principle involved in this bill because, as I see it, the principle is that there be equal status for the two languages where there is reasonable need for it. I suggest that, unfortunately, the debate in the House of Commons on this bill has concentrated on these other interpretations, and as a result, there has been a great deal of misunderstanding about the objectives of this measure. The most common misunderstanding is that the government of Canada is trying to force all Canadians to be bilingual. Perhaps even that is a little extreme. What the government is doing, in my opinion, is much more simple than that.
The aim of this legislation is to ensure that the English and French languages will have equal status throughout the federal government where conditions make that a reasonable requirement. What is even more important is that Canadians speaking either language will be treated in the same manner in their dealings with the federal government, wherever it is possible to do so.
What this means in practical terms as far as I understand it is that, firstly, in all parts of the country where there is a significant number of Canadians of both languages, the federal government will undertake to serve these people in both languages. I suppose the best example is in the national capital region, the Ottawa-Hull area, where people will be able to write or deal with a government office in either the French or the English language. In other words, they will have the opportunity to obtain service in the language of their choice.
If there are areas in Canada in which a significant part of the population wish to speak either one of the official languages,

then the government will try to provide services in that language. In Alberta, for example, there is only one area which has more than 10 per cent who are French speaking. As I understand the bill, this is the only area of that province which this provision would affect immediately. However, there may be a desire to have the services of the federal government extended somewhat beyond that in the future. I suggest that all Canadians in all areas should be able to deal with the government in either language. However, practically speaking, that is not possible. So, I suggest, that in the proposed legislation the government is trying to balance practicality with idealism.
The government has also undertaken to ensure that persons may be tried in federal criminal courts in either of the official languages. This is essential in my view if Canadians are to be guaranteed justice, again taking into consideration what is practical and feasible. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) announced some amendments he is prepared to make to the bill in that respect when it gets to the committee.
At the same time the legislation provides, and this has been overlooked too often I think, that merit will continue to be the basis for recruitment and promotion within the civil service rather than only proficiency in both languages. There are positions, of course, and all members of this house know this, where it is essential to be able to work in both languages. Bilingual proficiency in those cases will be considered when these jobs are filled.
I was rather surprised to hear one or two members who spoke this afternoon indicate that there was some kind of discrimination involved in requiring at least a reasonable level of proficiency in both languages on the part of those people who only have capability in one language. If the position requires the use of both languages, surely this should be a requisite for employment or, indeed, a promotion to that position. I do not think this should be regarded as discrimination. If there is a requirement for someone who can type, surely there is no discrimination in not hiring someone who cannot type. If the federal Government has a requirement for someone who can operate a particular piece of machinery, surely there is no discrimination in not hiring someone who does not have proficiency in this field. When a position requires proficiency in English, French or both, then it is not discrimination in any way to require that
May 26, 1969

the person applying for that position be proficient in those areas. An individual should have that proficiency before being considered for the position.
There are many who are opposed to this legislation, as has been indicated during this debate and indeed in the debate going on outside this institution. I suppose that is to be expected. On the other hand, I would hope that this opposition would be based on an accurate rather than a distorted picture of what this legislation is trying to do. I would also hope that any opposition would be based on a reasonable position rather than on an extreme emotional interpretation. That is all we are asking, and I think it is important to understand what is in the bill before it goes to the committee.
It has been said a number of times that Canada is a bilingual nation historically and traditionally. The legislation now before the house is an attempt to make that history and constitution a living reality in Canadian life. In conclusion, I do not think I could do better than to quote a paragraph from the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who I think did an excellent job of summing up his attitude toward this bill. He said as reported at page 8794 of Hansard for Friday, May 16:
I urge the government in the name of this country to make a serious effort to explain to the people of Canada what this bill means, what it does not mean, and to give the assurances to this country which are necessary for the administration and implementation of this measure. After all, we are trying to create unity, not disunity.
I think that is as good a statement of the position as one can find. Surely, this should be understood by those people who disagree with what is, in fact, the objective of the provisions of this bill. It is so important, as the Leader of the Opposition has stated, that the people of Canada understand what is involved. It behooves all of us on both sides of this house to explain the objective accurately to the people, without distorting it in any way. o (5:40 p.m.)

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this bill, I realize that contained in it is one of the most important principles which the people of this country must face up to and resolve if our country is to survive. The deputy leader of our party, speaking on second reading of the bill some days ago, put the position of our
Official Languages
party very clearly as one of support for the bill. I shall support this bill.
However, I want especially to take this opportunity to speak to it because, like so many other members from western Canada, I represent a constituency which has in it very few French speaking people. I represent a constituency in which the majority of the people are neither of French nor English extraction. More than 25 per cent of the people I represent are of Ukrainian origin, more than 10 per cent are of Polish origin and more than 10 per cent are of Jewish origin.
These people, as well as many Anglo-Saxons in my constituency and other parts of Canada, are dubious about this bill; they are worried and concerned about it. They feel very much as the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) feels about the bill. They feel, very much like the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), who spoke a short time ago, feels about the bill.
Despite that fact, I am prepared to vote for the bill. I want to explain today, as I have on every occasion when I have had the opportunity to speak to my constituents about this matter, why I feel that this kind of bill must be supported by the people of Canada. I do not think I can put my position in any better way than I did more than two years ago in response to a letter which I received from a man who was at that time one of my constituents.
I want, for a few moments, to read an exchange of correspondence which took place in March of 1967. I shall put on the record the letter 1 received from my constituent because it expresses the fears of many people in Canada. I shall also put on the record my reply because, as I have said, I do not think I can state my position any better today than I did more than two years ago. My constituent wrote me as follows:
Dear Mr. Orlikow:
I have talked to so many about how French is being driven down our throats these days. Everywhere you look or read it's in French and English, never just English anymore.
In the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation office here in Winnipeg I asked the girl at the desk for some information forms and she asked: "Can you speak French?" I said no, and didn't intend to learn. She said that was all they had available at this time. I said: "What is this country coming to?" She said: "You don't know the half of it. I am going to lose my job because I can't speak French."
I have a friend who works for Air Canada who is losing his job just because he can't speak French. We have so many different nationalities in Canada, why shove French down our throats?

May 26, 1969
Official Languages
I don't imagine anything can be done as all parties are strictly after the votes and will do the same thing but some day they may have to change if the people get mad enough about it. What can you do to bring Canada back to one language, like the Americans have?
I replied to that letter as follows:
Dear Sir:
The problem you raise in your letter is one of the most fundamental problems which this country will have to solve in the next few years if it is to survive.
I think that as a member of parliament whose ethnic origin is neither English nor French and who, therefore, understands the emotions which led you to express the views which you did, I am in a good position to explain what is happening in Canada and why, in regard to Quebec, I think we all have to realize that the French Canadians are in an entirely different position from those of us who are neither of English nor French origin.
When this country was formed in 1867, the BNA Act spelled out the rights of the French speaking people to use their language.
The French Canadians make up almost one-third of the population of Canada. They make up almost 80 per cent of the population of Quebec, and they make up about 45 per cent of the population of New Brunswick. There are very substantial numbers of French speaking Canadians in eastern and northern Ontario.
This being the case, it seems to me that we have to face the fact that whether some of us think that it would be better if everyone spoke one language or not, is really a theoretical matter because the fact is we cannot dictate such a policy to the five or six million French Canadians.
It seems to me, therefore, if we wish Canada to survive we must accept the fact the French Canadians, where they live in appreciable numbers, have a right to be dealt with by the government of Canada in the French language, just as English Canadians have a right to be dealt with in the English language.
This does not mean that every federal civil servant working in Winnipeg must be able to speak French, just as it does not mean that a federal civil servant working in a French community in rural Quebec must be able to speak English as well as French.
But it does mean that where there are an appreciable number of people who speak either English or French, they have a right to be served by government offices in their own language.
Now I would like to take up the specific cases in your letter. It may of course have been true that the CMHC office in Winnipeg was out of some form which you required in English, and that you were offered a form in French. I cannot however believe that a person working in the CMHC office in Winnipeg could have been serious when she told you that she was going to lose her job because she cannot speak French. There is no such government policy and there will be no such government policy.
If the girl is worried about losing her job and if she contacts me, I can assure you that within one day of receiving her letter she will have a statement in writing from the responsible minister

that as long as she works in Winnipeg she can keep her job without knowing French. I can assure you that the same is true of your friend who works for Air Canada who you say is losing his job because he cannot speak French.
I gather from the whole tenor of your letter, you feel the French are taking over the government of Canada. Recently the government was asked for information about the top servants-how many are French speaking and how many are English speaking.
The reply covered all federal civil servants earning $17,000 a year or more. The answer, I think, disproves completely the suggestion that this country is being taken over by French Canadians.
Of just over 1,100 civil servants making $17,000 or more, 975 list their mother tongue as English and only 136 list their mother tongue as French. In other words French Canadians occupy just 10 per cent of the top civil service jobs in Canada while they make up about 30 per cent of the population of Canada.
These are the facts as they are, rather than the misconceptions which so many of us have picked up on this emotionally charged question. It may be that you will not be too happy with my reply, but I think that we have to ignore immediate political advantage and face the realities of the. situation as they are.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
Nothing has happened in the last two and a half years to make me change my point of view. If this bill goes part of the way towards implementing the principle which I enunciated at that time, I am prepared to vote for it whether or not I think that in the short run my support of this bill may hurt me politically.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I was very pleased by a series of articles which appeared recently in the Toronto Telegram under the title "Canada 70". The articles constituted a survey done in considerable depth about how the people of Canada feel about this and related questions. I was pleased because, having just said that I would vote for this bill whether or not it hurt me politically, I am, after all, like every other member of this house, a practical politician who would like to be re-elected. So, if I get evidence to indicate that the people in my area tend to agree with me, it makes me happy.
I would like to summarize very briefly for the house, and particularly for those members of western Canada who seem to be worried that if they vote for this bill they may be going against the desires of the people they represent, some of the conclusions to which
May 26, 1969

this series of articles came. The following is from an article which appeared on May 6:
In talks with more than 100 people, Telegram interviewers found goodwill towards the aims of French Canada-
The citizens of Saskatchewan revealed a desire to hold this nation together, although they wanted it to be a nation with a better understanding of the western problems. The article contained the following statement:
But Saskatchewanians were overwhelmingly opposed to the idea of joining the United States, with 96 per cent voicing disdain.
Farther on it reads as follows:
A notable revelation in this province with its heavily ethnic population was the fact that 53 per cent are prepared to regard the French-speaking as special-
A healthy 75 per cent opted for bilingual education in the schools.
This is an indication of how the people of Saskatchewan feel.
In another article we are given some of the thinking in British Columbia. The article deals with educators in British Columbia. It reads in part as follows:
And 18 of 20 leading, interesting or controversial West coast educationists and student leaders agreed that it was very important to them that Canada survive as a nation-
And three quarters of them thought French Canadians rate a special place in Confederation, a considerably higher ratio than that found in the overall West coast population.
In an article in which they deal with Manitoba, the Telegram says:
And it was in Manitoba that the highest percentage of people consider that French Canadians have a special place in Confederation.
The figure was 62 per cent compared with 53 per cent in Saskatchewan and 48 per cent in Alberta.
As I said a few moments ago, these articles made me happy because they made me realize that the position I have taken is one which is shared by a majority of the people in western Canada.
Having said that I am going to support the bill, I want to deal with what I consider to be some of the negative aspects of the government's position. We have heard repeatedly that this bill is just one more indication of the overwhelming support which this government gives to the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Biculturalism and Bilingualism. It may be that in this bill the government is doing that. However, I want to suggest that this government and the Prime
Official Languages
Minister (Mr. Trudeau) cannot, without jettisoning a good deal of the basic convictions of the Prime Minister, endorse all the recommendations of the commission.
I want to refer the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) to the second volume of the commission's report, the volume which deals with education. I want to read just a couple of the recommendations which the Secretary of State may find on pages 301 and 302 of the report. They read as follows:
We recommend a federal grant to official minority-language students to enable them to study in their own language at a Canadian university outside their province, when courses are not available in their own language within the province.
We recommend for these out-of-province students that a federal grant, equivalent to the normal provincial grant to the university, be paid to the host university or to the provincial government concerned.
We recommend that, pending the resolution of the constitutional problems involved, agreements be concluded between the federal government and the provinces concerned in order that these provinces receive the help required to meet the special needs of their French-language universities.
Most important is recommendation 26 which can be found on page 302 of the second volume of the report of the commission. It reads as follows:
We recommend that the federal government accept in principle the responsibility for the additional costs involved in providing education in the official minority language.
Members of this house from various parties may or may not agree with that recommendation. I want to suggest, however, that if this government were to accept the recommendation, this would be completely contrary to the Prime Minister's stated policy. I understand, although I did not hear him, that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) indicated in his speech the other day that he is prepared to accept that kind of suggestion. I want to say that everything the Prime Minister has said and written before he came to parliament on the question of the constitution, and of the relationship between the federal government and the provinces, indicates clearly that he was absolutely opposed to the federal government contributing to education in any shape or form.
Let me quote from an article which the Prime Minister wrote before he came here, entitled "Federal Grants to Universities".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I concluded the section of my speech which I made before six o'clock I was pointing out that the second report of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Bicul-turalism had recommended that the federal government assist financially in the promotion of education for minority groups, that is, for French people living outside Quebec and for English people living in Quebec.
I submit that the position of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about which he spoke and wrote extensively both before and after coming into parliament is that he has always opposed the participation of the federal government in spheres of activity which are reserved to the provinces under the constitution. A book which was brought out a year or

so ago under the title "Federalism and French Canadians" contained articles written by the Prime Minister. In an article entitled "Federal Grants to Universities" the Prime Minister quotes with approval the position taken by Mr. F. A. Angers who said, and I quote:
In genera], the Canadian state is not the central government, but the central and the provincial governments taken together ... in matters of education the Canadian state is the provincial state, and none other.
Later in the same article, the Prime Minister said:
Consequently, if there is federal legislation to grant taxation money for provincial purposes, this legislation is illegal for the excellent reason that the federal government cannot by law have money in its coffers which it then claims should be used for provincial purposes.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if education is the responsibility of the provinces alone I find it hard to understand how the federal government can follow the recommendation of the B and B Commission and help finance the education of members of minority groups in the provinces. Having said this, I want to add that in my opinion the government should do so. If it did, then I submit the government could also assist the various ethnic groups in Canada by providing financial aid toward the maintenance and preservation of their cultures, their languages and their schools which they have developed on a voluntary basis.
If the federal government were to do this it would be following a line which the Prime Minister himself explored before he reached that office on the occasion of his visit to my own city of Winnipeg. In the Winnipeg Free Press, which, as I am sure hon. members are aware, is one of the most partisan Liberal partisan papers in the country, a report appeared on March 11, 1968, of an address to a meeting made by the Prime Minister in the course of that visit to Winnipeg. The title of the article was: "Trudeau Sees Four Official Languages if French Given Recognition". The report states:
Justice Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau said last night Canada may one day have a third and even a fourth official language in addition to English and French.
Trudeau, 46-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext: Forty-seven.

speechtext:
I am only reading the article. I cannot vouch for the veracity of every word.
-who becomes Prime Minister said official status should be granted any language spoken by a sufficient number of people.
May 26, 1969

The justice minister was addressing about 600 Liberals including representatives of Winnipeg's Ukrainian and other large ethnic minorities.
Trudeau rejected the common notion that French deserves official recognition in Canada because the French were one of the "two founding groups" which built the country-
The only justification for having French as official language was that French Canadians made up one third of the population, he added.
I would even be prepared to say that if in the immediate future or the far future a third important group speaking a third language wanted to use their language to communicate with the state, this third language will have to be recognized.
He said a fourth official language was also conceivable although "you can't go on forever." But Switzerland, he pointed out, functioned with four languages.
I suggest that the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) have a look a the recommendations made by Professor Rudnyckyj. I do not agree with everything that Professor Rudnyckyj proposes, but bearing in mind that in the Province of Manitoba from which I come more than 10 per cent of the population is Ukrainian, and further substantial parts of the population are of Polish or German extraction, to mention just a few of our minorities, I submit to the Secretary of State that it is just as reasonable for the federal government to provide financial assistance to help these groups and similar groups in other provinces to preserve the best of their culture, of their language and of their ethnic press which lately the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) has gone a long way to destroying. The Secretary of State might well consider giving these organizations financial assistance of the kind already given to the association in Manitoba which is concerning itself with the retention and promotion of the French language in the province of Manitoba.
Earlier in my speech I said I supported the principle of bilingualism and biculturalism, and that in these circumstances I would vote for the bill. I said, and am happy to say again, that in my opinion the majority of the people of Manitoba and western Canada generally will support the principle of this measure. They do so because they realize that this is part of the price of being Canadian; that it is part of the price of having a country extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific. However, they know that Quebeckers and the French people of Canada are not the only ones with problems. They know the people of the western provinces have problems, as do the people of both urban and rural Manitoba. They support this bill, I submit, expecting that just as they are prepared to co-operate
Official Languages
and support it as part of the price of being Canadian, so will the federal government give some consideration to their problems and needs.
e (8:10 p.m.)
To date I submit the government has not done so. If any member on the government side doubts that, I suggest he read the lead article that appeared in the Toronto Daily Star last Saturday, May 24, written by Peter Regenstreif, in which he analyses the result of a survey that he and his associates conducted for that newspaper. The headline of the article reads: "Trudeau is 'only fair' as P.M., voter survey indicates". I should just like to put on record a couple of paragraphs from this article:
After one year in office, Pierre Trudeau gets an "only fair" or "poor" rating from most of the Canadian electorate for the job he has been doing as Prime Minister, according to a national survey.
The public is disappointed with his handling of basic issues such as high taxes, the cost of living, housing and poverty.
Later, the article says:
Only 6 per cent gave Trudeau an "excellent" rating for the job he is doing as Prime Minister; 29 per cent gave him a "pretty good" rating, 34 per cent "only fair" and 23 per cent "poor" with 8 per cent not sure.
In every region, more people rated him as "only fair" and "poor" than graded him "excellent" and "pretty good." He is weakest on the prairies, strongest in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces-
Trudeau received very low grades for the job he is doing "keeping taxes in line" with 65 per cent giving him a "poor" rating. Another 65 per cent feel he is doing a poor job "controlling the cost of living".
His performance in "getting more housing and less expensive housing" and in "closing the gap between rich and poor" is ranked as poor by 54 per cent in each case. And 41 per cent says he is doing a "poor" job "alleviating poverty."
I think the result of that survey goes a long way to demonstrate precisely the point I am making. We are approaching the end of this session of parliament. There is no provision in the rules or statutes which decrees we must finish this session on June 27, yet we are told that this will happen. But what will we have accomplished at this session of parliament? We will have passed the omnibus bill amending the Criminal Code, a bill that we in this party supported almost unanimously. I presume we will also have passed this official languages bill that we are now discussing, and which we in this party will support. But having said that, 1 have said just about everything that could be said.

May 26, 1969
Official Languages
I do not want to misrepresent the tacts or let anybody miscontrue my feelings, because these are two important pieces of legislation, measures that were long overdue for passage. But as far as the ordinary citizen of Canada is concerned, regardless of province, whether he is English, French or a member of what we call the third force, these are not bread and butter issues. Since the government was elected last year it has refused to deal with basic issues, such as the increasing cost of living and the galloping inflation with which we are faced.
What is the Prime Minister's solution to inflation? He has gone back to Herbert Hoover, perhaps even before Hoover. His answer to inflation is to cut government expenditure. Apparently it does not matter how important those government programs are; they are going to be cut. At the same time we permit builders to build fancy office buildings, oil companies to build a filling station on a corner where there are already three other filling stations, and every grocery chain to build another supermarket, even though in Ottawa there is but five minutes' walk from one to another. We permit these people to do exactly what they please while we try to beat inflation by cutting down government expenditure.
The Secretary of State once worked for a trade union and used to know, if he does not know any more, how ordinary people live and work. The kind of issue I suggest the government ought to be dealing with relates to the fact, hundreds of thousands of people are living in dilapidated housing, in housing that is a disgrace.
